title: Predictions for 2026 in AI and the Law — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source expects continued change in AI and law and proposes revisiting forecasts, aligning with the cluster’s emphasis on ongoing reassessment. However, it does not address whether lawyers should actively shape AI deployment, support implementation, or participate in governance, so its position on the principal engagement-first proposition cannot be determined.
qs: But one thing's for sure: the world of AI and the law is not slowing down.We’ve had a great time this season exploring it with all of you.
We'll have to touch back next year at this time to see how we did.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source accepts that AI-era junior development requires deliberate redesign and adds concrete mechanisms: substantial protected time for AI learning and personalised formative coaching for junior lawyers. It strengthens the cluster’s implementation case, although it does not directly establish the core causal claim that automation is removing the work through which expertise was traditionally acquired.
qs: Ropes & Gray just made a big announcement last month that they are allocating 400 hours for their first years toward their billable requirements for first-years to experiment with AI and to learn how to work alongside it.
Since the beginning of the GenAI era, my favorite use case has been using it for more formative coaching—especially in law school and the junior years.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source accepts that AI adoption creates a talent-development and institutional-change challenge, then materially extends the cluster with concrete responses: protected billable-credit time for first-year AI learning, structured AI-aware recruitment, and durable C-suite change leadership. Its claims about broader platform restructuring remain tentative and informally evidenced.
qs: Ropes & Gray just made a big announcement last month that they are allocating 400 hours for their first years toward their billable requirements for first-years to experiment with AI and to learn how to work alongside it.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source accepts that AI creates an expertise-development challenge and materially extends the proposition with a concrete funding mechanism: protected first-year hours for AI learning. It also predicts accelerated professional development and identifies AI capability as a recruitment criterion, though these remain programme reports and forecasts rather than evidence of improved competence or succession outcomes.
qs: Ropes & Gray just made a big announcement last month that they are allocating 400 hours for their first years toward their billable requirements for first-years to experiment with AI and to learn how to work alongside it.
So there’ll be a lot of accelerated professional development happening.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: McCormack materially extends the cluster’s account of converging providers and potential new capital structures by forecasting a specific capital-backed ecosystem: MSOs as infrastructure, ALSPs as the legal-production layer, and AI as the scaling mechanism. This is a prospective model based on investor interest rather than demonstrated market outcomes.
qs: I think the combination of—the interest of capital in our business—and AI's ability to scale some of the solutions that MSOs and ALSPs were providing to lawyers is really going to move us quickly, and I think we'll start to see this even next year, into a platformization of law.You'll see a combination of those, where MSOs could be the infrastructure layer.

I don't mean AI-native law firms—we've already seen those in 2025—I mean something larger, like these integrated ecosystems where a combination of MSOs and ALSPs and this strong interest from capital is fueling some consolidation.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source accepts active engagement with legal AI while materially extending the cluster’s reform agenda into a concrete research program: compare access to legal information with and without AI and begin collecting outcome data. It treats benefits as hypotheses requiring evidence, consistent with redesign and experimentation before technological certainty rather than reliance on analogy or prediction alone.
qs: And I feel like we could have similar findings about legal information, right?If there were a way to collect and release data for researchers to make some sense of the difference between access to legal information—both rights and responsibilities and legal processes—with AI versus without it, it seems like such a significant difference that it might accelerate some adoption across the legal profession.
I would love to see some data around AI outcomes.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source accepts that AI value depends on organisational redesign and materially extends the cluster by proposing an integrated production architecture spanning MSOs, ALSPs and law firms, alongside accelerated training, structured AI-talent assessment and C-suite change leadership. Its platformisation claims remain forecasts grounded mainly in industry observation rather than systematic outcome evidence.

I think we're at a stage where it's become clear to me that AI is here to stay, and you need somebody who is an expert in change management and can translate across the practice side and the business side, and should sit at the C-suite level to oversee all of these things.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts that AI will restructure legal-service production while preserving valuable human legal work, and materially extends the cluster by forecasting an integrated platform model in which MSOs provide infrastructure, ALSPs deliver AI-enabled production, and smaller firms supply differentiated human services. It also develops the cluster’s talent theme through concrete firm training investments and expected demand for AI-skilled lawyers, though its market-wide claims remain primarily predictions and anecdotal observations.
qs: I don't mean AI-native law firms—we've already seen those in 2025—I mean something larger, like these integrated ecosystems where a combination of MSOs and ALSPs and this strong interest from capital is fueling some consolidation.

Then I think law firms—not necessarily the Am Law 100, but smaller law firms—could plug into these platforms and provide the unique human services that lawyers will continue to provide and which will be, maybe, more and more valuable.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source accepts legal AI as organisational change rather than a software purchase and materially develops that proposition with concrete prescriptions: protected experimentation time and C-suite leadership combining change management with practice-business coordination. Its hiring, training and flexible-governance proposals further connect adoption to incentives, capabilities and professional development, though several broader outcomes remain predictions.
qs: Ropes & Gray just made a big announcement last month that they are allocating 400 hours for their first years toward their billable requirements for first-years to experiment with AI and to learn how to work alongside it.

I think we're at a stage where it's become clear to me that AI is here to stay, and you need somebody who is an expert in change management and can translate across the practice side and the business side, and should sit at the C-suite level to oversee all of these things.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the need for supervision, outcome evidence and cautious, use-specific deployment, then materially extends the cluster by proposing bounded opt-in AI adjudication pilots with human appeal and data collection. Its platformisation claims also anticipate operating-model redesign, though these remain predictions rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: Okay, my final one is: I think 2026 is a year where we will start to see some very experimental, opt-in—both parties have to agree—court AI resolution for certain low-stakes, high-volume matters.
Courts can therefore structure experiments in a way where parties can have an appeal to a human judge if they are dissatisfied with it.

st.t: AI competition: Distribution and habits rival capability
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s framing by combining Google’s ecosystem, infrastructure and revenue advantages with Gemini 3’s reported agentic and benchmark gains. Its strong competitive claims remain qualified by limited firsthand testing and uncertainty about whether public enthusiasm reflects genuine experience.
qs: We're all in Google all the time—our Gmail and our Docs; so much of our lives they have access to.
I sort of regularly use ChatGPT 5.1 and Gemini 3.I don't know that I personally am using it for the kinds of things that would show it off the way others have.

st.t: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison
st.an: The source supports assessing bounded court AI experimentation against unmet party needs and persistent court-capacity problems. It proposes opt-in pilots for limited case types, human appeal and evidence collection, while presenting these as predictions and tests rather than proof of improved outcomes.
qs: Okay, my final one is: I think 2026 is a year where we will start to see some very experimental, opt-in—both parties have to agree—court AI resolution for certain low-stakes, high-volume matters.
But it’s a way to start figuring out where AI adjudication can help parties and therefore help courts manage dockets that have been hard for them to manage for a long time—at state courts, at least.

kp.k: Agentic AI shifts from conversation toward task execution
kp.d: Leonard describes Gemini 3 as combining reasoning, native multimodality and Antigravity tool access to execute high-level goals, rather than merely respond conversationally. She reports leadership on Humanity's Last Exam and visual-reasoning scores nearly double ChatGPT 5.1, but supplies no benchmark methodology or underlying results. Both speakers qualify their personal experience as not involving the most complex advertised tasks.
qs: It has direct access to a code editor, a terminal, and a browser. So you tell it a high-level goal, and it handles the implementation of how to execute that goal.
It's been scoring really well on the benchmarks for visual reasoning—nearly double the ChatGPT 5.1 score.
First, we're moving away from the “chat era,” where we're just chatting with an AI, to an era where the AIs are acting more agentic and able to execute on our goals.
I don't know that I personally am using it for the kinds of things that would show it off the way others have.

kp.k: Integrated resources shape competition among AI suppliers
kp.d: McCormack argues that Google's existing user data, cloud, chips and research lab position it for sustained AI competition. Leonard adds established revenue, product integration and perceived management discipline, contrasting these with OpenAI and Anthropic's still-evolving startup business models. These are the speakers' strategic assessments, not demonstrated findings about legal-market outcomes.
qs: But I always figured they'd be here, because they have so much of our data already at their fingertips, right?
And they also have a cloud; OpenAI doesn't.
In addition to all the things that you mentioned, the other thing is they have an enormous revenue stream that they can use to fund all of their AI efforts.
They're hugely valuable companies, but they're startups, and they have not yet figured out their business model.

kp.k: Comparative outcomes research could support legal AI adoption
kp.d: McCormack uses a physician's New York Times discussion of Waymo safety data as an analogy for comparing access to legal information with and without AI. She reports the physician's claim that the safety benefit would make withholding treatment unethical in a drug experiment, then proposes collecting and releasing legal outcomes data for researchers. Neither speaker presents an equivalent legal study; the anticipated adoption benefit remains hypothetical.
qs: This physician looked at it for many, many weeks and compared it to data of human-driven cars.
he was saying that if this was an ongoing experiment with a new drug and you had this kind of success with it, it would be unethical to keep giving the placebo to anybody

If there were a way to collect and release data for researchers to make some sense of the difference between access to legal information—both rights and responsibilities and legal processes—with AI versus without it, it seems like such a significant difference that it might accelerate some adoption across the legal profession.

kp.k: Capital could consolidate AI-native legal delivery platforms
kp.d: McCormack predicts beginnings of legal-market platformization in 2026, combining private equity, MSOs as infrastructure providers and ALSPs as producers of specialized AI-enabled legal services. Infrastructure would include automation, compliance, knowledge management and analytics; production could include discovery, contracting and document workflows. She distinguishes these integrated ecosystems from AI-native law firms already seen in 2025, suggesting smaller firms could connect to them while supplying distinctively human services. Leonard supports the reported capital interest with headlines and informal conversations, not quantified investment evidence.
qs: we're seeing significant private equity interest in the business of law—specifically in MSOs and ALSPs.
You'll see a combination of those, where MSOs could be the infrastructure layer.
Then I think the ALSPs can become the production layer.

I don't mean AI-native law firms—we've already seen those in 2025—I mean something larger, like these integrated ecosystems where a combination of MSOs and ALSPs and this strong interest from capital is fueling some consolidation.

Then I think law firms—not necessarily the Am Law 100, but smaller law firms—could plug into these platforms and provide the unique human services that lawyers will continue to provide and which will be, maybe, more and more valuable.

kp.k: Entry-level preparation gaps could accelerate employer training
kp.d: Leonard predicts that law schools' lag in preparing graduates for AI will become apparent to employers in 2026, prompting accelerated professional development. As a reported investment example, she cites Ropes & Gray's announcement the previous month allocating 400 hours toward first-year billable requirements for AI experimentation and learning. She estimates the firm's annual requirement at about 1,900 hours; the transcript provides no assessment of training outcomes.
qs: I think when new lawyers get to their places of employment, it will soon become evident that new lawyers are not as prepared as people expected them to be.

Ropes & Gray just made a big announcement last month that they are allocating 400 hours for their first years toward their billable requirements for first-years to experiment with AI and to learn how to work alongside it.
At a firm where I think they have about 1,900 billable hours a year, to allocate 400 of those toward that is huge.

kp.k: Recruitment increasingly requires explicit AI competency assessment
kp.d: Drawing on her firm's workshops and professional conversations, Leonard describes a two-sided lateral recruitment challenge: signaling that a firm is AI-forward while assessing partners' and senior associates' AI skills. She recommends structured competency matrices for interviews instead of informal alumni conversations. A November advertisement for 1L summer positions before candidates' first examinations illustrates how early firms are trying to assess potential.
qs: Our team has been running workshops with firms to think about both how firms are signaling to the marketplace that they are AI-forward when they're looking for laterals, and, equally important, how they are trying to suss out from the marketplace that they are attracting partners and senior associates who have AI skills—and what that process looks like.

You really need to look under the hood and equip your lawyers with some sort of matrix that they go in with: questions and competencies that they're trying to evaluate during interviews that are now happening.
They have not even taken their first set of exams yet, and you're trying to assess all of this so early.

kp.k: AI leadership needs durable roles and executive authority
kp.d: Leonard says early AI leadership positions were often poorly designed, with frustration or competing compensation prompting departures and loss of institutional progress. She predicts more intentional role design and retention in 2026, and recommends C-suite leadership combining change-management expertise with the ability to connect legal practice and business operations.
qs: Those positions were not very well-designed in the first couple of years, but people were leading them and making progress, and then either becoming frustrated or being attracted by higher salaries or better packages at other firms and leaving—and losing all of that energy and progress.
So I think firms are going to be much more intentional in 2026 about structuring those positions well to keep that talent in-house and having a better sense of what they're actually looking for.
you need somebody who is an expert in change management and can translate across the practice side and the business side, and should sit at the C-suite level to oversee all of these things.

kp.k: Legal digital twins could scale expertise and mentorship
kp.d: McCormack explicitly frames digital twins of elite lawyers as an aspirational idea rather than a confident prediction. She envisages training on their writing, arguments, internal work and articulated reasoning to support continuous drafting, review, strategy and junior mentorship, with subscriptions or a marketplace extending expertise beyond hourly availability. She acknowledges unspecified hard questions. Leonard endorses formative coaching and suggests lawyer-number document storage could support personalized junior-lawyer coaches; no implemented system or measured performance is established.
qs: Maybe this isn't a prediction; maybe this is, “I think I have great ideas, so it should be a prediction—somebody should do it.”
I don't mean just a chatbot, but a fully realized digital version of that superstar lawyer's legal mind.

But the digital-twin Lisa Blatt could draft 24 hours a day, spot issues, supervise real Lisa Blatt's work, ask Lisa Blatt-like questions of Lisa Blatt’s drafts, run strategy sessions, and even act as a partner or mentor to more of the up-and-coming lawyers who have to learn how to do things in new ways.
You could imagine subscription versions for a Paul Clement twin, or use cases like brief review or moot court prep.
They store them by lawyer number. So if Bridget McCormack is a partner, you can customize a “Bridget McCormack coach” for your juniors and they can access her anytime, and I think that's amazing.

kp.k: Creativity could benefit from changing regulatory and career boundaries
kp.d: Leonard predicts that creative lawyers will benefit in 2026 from the combination of technological capability, regulatory liberalization and demand for different career paths. She presents this as an opportunity for experimentation, without specifying jurisdictions, rule changes or measured competitive advantages.
qs: there are spaces to be creative because of the regulatory liberalization and the technology and the people who are wanting different career paths.
So I think that 2026 will belong to the creatives.

kp.k: AI co-mediators could improve preparation while preserving human judgment
kp.d: McCormack proposes AI co-mediators that work separately with parties before mediation to clarify goals, emotional concerns and disagreements, then give the human mediator a stronger starting point. She predicts time and potential cost savings, greater satisfaction and more successful mediation, but offers no outcome evidence. Her model augments rather than replaces mediators, reserving work she expects humans to perform better for a long time.
qs: So before the mediation begins, each party gets to work with the co-mediator first to make sure that they feel understood and heard, and that their goals are very clear.
It would give the human mediator a real advantage in doing the work that the human mediator is going to be able to do better than an AI—in my view, at least for a long time.
I think it likely makes mediations significantly more successful and parties significantly more satisfied.

So I think every mediator is going to have an AI co-mediator to help them with the parts of the work that can be done just as well, and therefore allow them to really focus on the parts that the human is going to do so much better.

kp.k: AI pilots need defined objectives and systematic ROI measurement
kp.d: Leonard predicts more rigorous ROI methodologies in 2026, with pilot objectives specified at the outset, systematic information gathering and success assessed against those objectives. She also expects deeper applications beyond email refinement and document summarization. This is a forecast and methodological recommendation, not a reported return-on-investment finding.
qs: I think we'll start to see the emergence of more rigorous methodologies for measuring ROI.

everybody out there who is starting pilots will start at the beginning with better measures of what they're trying to get out of a pilot and more systematic ways of gathering that information and assessing whether it's successful
I think we'll also see deeper use cases versus just having everybody get onto the platforms to refine their emails and summarize documents—taking it a little bit further.

kp.k: Competency and verification frameworks risk constraining experimentation
kp.d: Leonard expects frameworks defining AI-use competency and human supervision of output, including checking argument logic and hallucinations. She welcomes this development but warns that lawyers may treat a single industry framework as permanently authoritative, ending the exploratory approach she values.
qs: What does competency look like when using AI? How do we supervise output to make sure that the underlying logic of the arguments is sound, that there aren't hallucinations—those kinds of things?
My hope is that people don't feel tethered to some sort of industry standard that stifles innovation and doesn't allow them to continue to explore.
My one negative prediction for 2026 is that we glom onto one thing and that is the end of our exploratory phase.

kp.k: Opt-in AI adjudication pilots could address court backlogs
kp.d: McCormack predicts experimental court AI resolution in 2026 for certain low-stakes, high-volume matters, conditional on both parties agreeing and with potential appeal to a human judge. She envisages qualitative and probably quantitative evidence from pilots to identify suitable cases and help state courts manage difficult dockets. She identifies no jurisdiction or existing pilot and describes the proposal as ODR 2.0.
qs: I think 2026 is a year where we will start to see some very experimental, opt-in—both parties have to agree—court AI resolution for certain low-stakes, high-volume matters.
Courts can therefore structure experiments in a way where parties can have an appeal to a human judge if they are dissatisfied with it.
I don't know where we'll see it, but there will be some innovators out there who will stand up some of these pilots.
We'll start to be able to collect some information—qualitative and probably quantitative—as a result of some of those pilots.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Bridget McCormack predicts that AI and private capital will begin creating integrated legal-service platforms in 2026.
pts.d: McCormack envisages management services organizations (MSOs) supplying infrastructure such as workflow automation, compliance engines, knowledge management and analytics, while ALSPs deliver specialized AI-enabled work, including discovery and contracting. Private equity would accelerate integration, consolidation and scale. Smaller law firms could plug into these ecosystems and concentrate on distinctive human services, potentially increasing the value of those services. She distinguishes these platforms from AI-native law firms, which she says already appeared in 2025, and does not primarily target the AmLaw 100. Her basis is perceived investment interest and AI's scaling potential rather than quantified market evidence. Leonard adds observations from headlines, Jordan Furlong's writing and informal conversations.

pts.k: Jen Leonard predicts accelerated training for entry-level lawyers because law schools are lagging behind AI-driven workplace change.
pts.d: In her 2026 talent forecast, Leonard expects employers to discover that new lawyers are less prepared than anticipated and to expand professional development. As a concrete example of investment, she reports that Ropes & Gray announced 400 hours counting toward first-year billable requirements for AI experimentation and learning. She estimates the firm's annual billable requirement at about 1,900 hours. This is a reported firm initiative, not evidence of measured training outcomes or a quantified law-school preparedness gap.

pts.k: Jen Leonard expects AI competence to reshape recruitment, lateral hiring and retention of AI leadership.
pts.d: Leonard describes firms both signaling that they are AI-forward and trying to assess AI skills in prospective partners and senior associates. She argues for competency-based interviewing rather than conventional informal conversations, including in increasingly early student recruitment. She predicts more intentional design of AI leadership positions in 2026 to prevent departures that dissipate organizational progress. Her related recommendation is a C-suite-level leader with change-management expertise who can translate between practice and business. Evidence consists of her team's firm workshops, professional conversations, a recruitment advertisement and observations of leadership turnover; no systematic hiring or retention data are supplied.

pts.k: Bridget McCormack proposes digital twins of elite lawyers that could scale expertise beyond the lawyer's available hours and support new subscription businesses.
pts.d: McCormack imagines training a digital version of a lawyer on writing, oral arguments, internal memoranda, strategic decisions and explanations of legal problems. Suggested functions include continuous drafting, issue spotting, reviewing the original lawyer's work, strategy sessions, mentoring, brief review and moot-court preparation. She imagines eventual subscriptions and a marketplace of elite digital legal minds. She explicitly qualifies this as possibly an idea someone should pursue rather than a firm prediction, acknowledges unspecified hard questions and offers no demonstrated implementation or performance evidence. It appears in the 2026 discussion, but the marketplace is described as eventual.

pts.k: Jen Leonard argues that firms' lawyer-indexed document collections make them well positioned to provide personalized AI coaching for juniors.
pts.d: Responding to the digital-twin proposal, Leonard identifies formative coaching in law school and the junior years as a favored use case. She says documents stored by lawyer number could support a coach modeled on an individual partner, available whenever juniors need it. Her basis is a stated characteristic of firm document organization and her experience of the use case, not a study of learning outcomes. This is presented as an available opportunity, without a specific deployment deadline.

pts.k: Jen Leonard predicts that creative lawyers will gain particular advantages in 2026.
pts.d: Leonard argues that AI expands what creative professionals can execute, while regulatory liberalization and demand for different career paths create additional opportunities. She draws on creativity workshops her team runs, without quantifying commercial or professional gains. The forecast is broad rather than a specified market-share or productivity prediction; no particular regulatory regime is identified.

pts.k: Bridget McCormack predicts AI co-mediators will improve preparation, reduce time and costs, and increase mediation success and party satisfaction.
pts.d: McCormack proposes separate preparatory interactions between each party and an AI co-mediator to clarify goals, disagreements and emotional concerns before the human-led mediation. The AI would give the mediator greater clarity and a stronger starting point, allowing the human to focus on work she expects humans to do better for a long time. This is an augmentation model, not replacement of the mediator. Her forecast rests on professional reasoning about mediation workflows, with no pilot results, cost estimates, settlement rates or satisfaction measurements supplied. The prediction occurs in the 2026 segment, but her broader expectation that every mediator will have a co-mediator has no explicit completion date.

pts.k: Jen Leonard predicts more rigorous AI return-on-investment measurement and deeper applications in 2026.
pts.d: Leonard expects pilots to begin with clearer intended outcomes, systematic information collection and assessment against their original objectives. She also expects use to move beyond email refinement and document summarization. Her basis is an assessment that the industry is not accustomed to systematic pilot measurement; she does not provide ROI figures, a survey or named examples demonstrating this transition. Firms and other legal organizations running pilots are the immediate affected actors.

pts.k: Jen Leonard predicts AI competency and output-verification frameworks, while warning that rigid standardization could suppress experimentation.
pts.d: Leonard expects frameworks addressing competent AI use and human supervision of outputs for sound legal reasoning and hallucinations. These concern professional competence and verification, not model benchmarking. Her negative 2026 prediction is that lawyers may treat a single framework as permanently authoritative and end the exploratory phase. The basis is her characterization of lawyers' tendency to adhere rigidly to standards, not evidence from a specific framework or measured incident series.

pts.k: Bridget McCormack predicts experimental court AI adjudication pilots in 2026 for selected low-stakes, high-volume disputes.
pts.d: McCormack limits the forecast to voluntary experiments requiring both parties' agreement and describes a possible appeal to a human judge. She expects pilots to help identify where AI resolution benefits parties and eases persistent docket-management problems, particularly in state courts, while generating qualitative and probably quantitative evidence. She calls this ODR 2.0 and anticipates eventual usefulness for some cases and parties, not universal replacement of judges. She names no jurisdiction or existing pilot supporting the forecast.

pts.k: Bridget McCormack suggests comparative evidence could reveal substantial benefits from AI-assisted access to legal information and accelerate professional adoption.
pts.d: McCormack proposes comparing access to information about rights, responsibilities and legal processes with and without AI. Her reasoning is analogical: she recounts a New York Times physician's discussion of Waymo safety data and asks whether law could produce similarly persuasive comparisons. No legal-outcome dataset or demonstrated legal benefit is presented. The claim is conditional on collecting and releasing data for researchers; Leonard endorses the desire for legal-system outcome evidence. The affected groups are people seeking legal information and legal professionals deciding whether to adopt AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The legal forecasts rely mainly on professional observations, workflow reasoning and proposed possibilities rather than measured legal outcomes.
pts.d: The strongest concrete legal-sector example supplied is Leonard's report of Ropes & Gray's training allocation. Other support includes workshops, professional conversations, investment headlines and experience with mediation workflows. Digital twins and AI adjudication are forward-looking proposals without demonstrated implementations in the transcript. The discussion of Gemini 3 cites general technology benchmarks, including Humanity's Last Exam and an unnamed visual-reasoning comparison, but does not establish performance on legal tasks or evidence for the legal forecasts. The Waymo comparison is an analogy and motivation to gather legal evidence, not legal evidence itself.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The principal horizon is 2026, generally framed as the beginning of change rather than completed transformation.
pts.d: Platforms, talent changes, creativity advantages, measurement frameworks and court pilots are framed as 2026 developments. The digital-twin marketplace is eventual and expressly speculative. Universal co-mediator adoption has no firm deadline. Platform formation depends on capital integration and AI scalability; coaching depends on usable lawyer-specific materials; legal-information benefits require comparative data; court resolution is restricted to selected matters with both parties opting in and a possible human appeal. McCormack explicitly preserves a substantial human role in mediation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The anticipated effects span legal providers, legal talent, dispute-resolution professionals, courts and people using legal services.
pts.d: MSOs, ALSPs and investors could build integrated delivery platforms; smaller firms could gain scalable infrastructure while retaining human-specialist work. Students and junior lawyers face new competence requirements and expanded training or coaching. Lateral candidates and AI leaders face changed recruitment and role design. Elite lawyers could extend and monetize expertise through digital twins. Mediators and disputants could benefit from better preparation, reduced time and greater satisfaction. State courts and consenting parties in selected low-stakes disputes could test AI resolution. People seeking legal information are potential beneficiaries of improved access, distinct from enterprise efficiency savings.
